questions.stem: void grow(Box b, int n) { b.size += n; } with b.size 4; after grow(b,3) what is b.size?

options.text: 4 because the reference is passed by value.
options.misconception: confuses reference passing with mutation visibility

options.text: 7 because the shared object is mutated.
3 because only n is used.
0 because b is reassigned.

questions.explanation: The reference copy points to the same object, so mutating b.size changes the shared object. The caller sees 7.
questions.hint: Mutation through a shared reference is visible.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: Compare two references for identity
questions.stem: Box a = new Box(1); Box b = new Box(1); what is (a == b)?

options.text: true because both have size 1.
true because new Box is interned.
false because they are distinct objects.
false only if equals is overridden.

questions.explanation: == compares references, and the two new expressions create distinct objects, so the result is false. equals would compare contents if overridden.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: Choose a useful toString format
questions.stem: Which toString output is most helpful for debugging a Point?

options.text: The class name repeated ten times.
The default hash code only.
An empty string to save space.
"Point(x=3, y=4)" showing field names and values.

questions.explanation: Including field names and values makes the output informative. The default hash code is opaque and less useful for debugging.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: Maintain the toString contract
questions.stem: What should an overridden toString generally return?

options.text: A concise, informative string representation of the object.
null to signal no representation.
The memory address of the object.

questions.explanation: toString should return a readable representation. Returning null or an address is unhelpful and may cause errors in concatenation.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: Handle null in equals
questions.stem: public boolean equals(Object o) { return this.size == ((Box)o).size; } has what bug?

options.text: The bug is comparing ints with ==.
It is fine because null casts to Box.
It throws when o is null because of the cast.
No bug exists because equals handles null automatically.

questions.explanation: Casting null to Box succeeds, but accessing .size on null throws NullPointerException. Add a null check before casting.

questions.learningObjective: Compute a simple hashCode
questions.stem: If hashCode returns size * 31 and size is 4, what is the hashCode?
questions.explanation: 4 times 31 equals 124. This is a common multiplier pattern for hash codes.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: Intern a string explicitly
questions.stem: To make s1 == s2 true for two content-equal strings, call ??? on one of them.

options.text: s1.clone() copies the object.
s1.toLowerCase() normalizes case only.
s1.trim() removes whitespace only.
s1.intern() returns the interned reference.

questions.explanation: intern returns a reference from the string pool, so equal interned strings share one reference and == returns true.
questions.hint: Use intern to pool the string.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: Chain calls that return this
questions.stem: If builder.setX(1).setY(2) returns the same builder each time, how many objects are created?

options.text: Two new builders, one per call.
One builder reused throughout the chain.
Zero because setters are void.
Three builders including the original.

questions.explanation: Fluent setters returning this reuse the same object, so the chain creates no new builders beyond the original.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: Avoid using a void result in an expression
questions.stem: Which expression is illegal: int total = add(1,2) + multiply(3,4) where add is void?

options.text: The + operator cannot add ints.
multiply(3,4) is the illegal part.
add(1,2) cannot be used in arithmetic because it returns void.
No expression is illegal.

questions.explanation: A void method yields no value, so it cannot appear in an arithmetic expression. Only multiply's result can be used.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: Use a ternary to ensure a return
questions.stem: Complete the method body with a single return: int abs(int n) { return ???; }

options.text: return -n; negates always.
return (n >= 0) ? n : 0; drops the magnitude for negatives.
return n; ignores the sign entirely.
return (n >= 0) ? n : -n; returns n or its negation.

questions.explanation: The ternary returns n when non-negative and -n otherwise, covering both paths in one expression.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: Print then return without changing the value
questions.stem: int f(int x) { System.out.println(x); return ???; } should return the same x.

options.text: return x + 1; returns a different value.
return x; returns the printed value.
return 0; discards x.
return; invalid for int method.

questions.explanation: Returning x matches the printed value. Any other expression would make print and return disagree.
questions.hint: Return the same variable you printed.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: Avoid assuming memoization
questions.stem: A method with no side effects is called twice with the same argument. Are the results guaranteed equal?

options.text: No, the second call returns null.
No, Java re-evaluates randomly.
Yes, pure methods return the same result for the same input.
Yes only if the method is static.

questions.explanation: A pure, deterministic method returns the same value for equal inputs. Java does not introduce randomness between calls.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: Return a value on all paths including catch
questions.stem: int parse(String s) { try { return Integer.parseInt(s); } catch (Exception e) { System.out.println("bad"); } } fails because?

options.text: The method should be void.
parseInt never throws.
try cannot contain return.
The catch block does not return an int.

questions.explanation: If parsing throws, the catch block prints and falls through without returning. Add return 0; (or another default) in the catch.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: Overload resolution by parameter types
questions.stem: Given overloads print(int) and print(double), which is called by print(2)?

options.text: print(double) because int widens to double.
print(int) because 2 is an int literal.
Neither; the call is ambiguous.
Both are called in sequence.

questions.explanation: The compiler chooses the most specific matching overload, so the exact int match wins over the widening conversion to double.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: Recognize a discarded return value
questions.stem: Which line discards a return value: list.add(item); int size = list.size();?

options.text: list.size() discards its int result.
list.add(item) discards a boolean return.
Neither discards a value; both are used appropriately.
Both lines discard values.

questions.explanation: add's boolean return is often intentionally ignored, and size's result is assigned. Neither line is necessarily a bug in typical usage.
questions.hint: Consider whether the return is needed.

questions.learningObjective: Compute with a helper before returning
questions.stem: int g(int n) { int r = n + 1; return r * 2; } what is g(3)?

options.text: 6 because 3+1+2.
7 because 3+1*2.

questions.explanation: r becomes 4, then 4*2 is 8. The helper computation and final multiplication produce 8.

questions.learningObjective: Avoid long parameter lists
questions.stem: A method with many parameters is hard to call correctly mainly because?

options.text: It compiles more slowly.

questions.explanation: Long parameter lists increase the chance of swapping or misinterpreting arguments. Grouping into objects helps.

questions.stem: A switch on a type code inside a method can be refactored to?

More type codes and deeper nesting.
Polymorphic methods on subclasses or interfaces.
Static fields holding the type.
